sections.title_en: The Beit Din in the Conversion Process
sections.body_en:
Although the essence of conversion is accomplished by the convert, who chooses to join the people of Israel, which is destined to bring the word of God and His blessing to the world, the conversion must be carried out before a beit din (rabbinical court). This is because changing the status of the convert is a legal act that has consequences for all of Israel, and therefore the conversion must be carried out by a beit din (Yevamot 47a). However, a small Sanhedrin of twenty-three judges is not required for this; rather, a beit din of three judges suffices, which is the smallest judicial bench that exists in Jewish law (Yevamot 46b; Sanhedrin 3a).1

The beit din is needed for all stages of the conversion. In the first stage, the beit din examines the convert's desire to enter the people of Israel and to accept the Torah and the mitzvot, and decides whether to accept him. In the second stage, the beit din must be present at the time of the brit mila (circumcision) for men, and at the time of the immersion for men and women. For since the conversion depends on circumcision and immersion, they too are included in the judicial act of conversion, and they must take place before a beit din of three. Therefore, one must also take care that the brit mila and the immersion take place during the day, for since conversion is considered a "judgment" (mishpat), just as the judgments of the Torah, including the session of the beit din to accept the convert, must take place during the day, so too all stages of the conversion must take place during the day (SA YD 268:3).2

notes_en.en:
Yevamot 47a: "The Rabbis taught: 'And judge righteously between a man and his brother, and his convert (gero)' (Devarim 1:16) – from here Rabbi Yehuda said: A convert who converted before a beit din is a convert; by himself, he is not a convert." Another verse was cited by Rashi and Tosafot (ibid. 46b, s.v. "mishpat") as a source for this: "One Torah and one law (mishpat) shall be for you and for the convert who dwells with you" (Bamidbar 15:16). Admittedly, these verses do not deal with conversion, but only with the need to judge converts like all of Israel; however, we learn from them that following conversion, converts acquire a legal status like all of Israel, and consequently it is understood that the conversion itself must also have legal validity.
The Aḥaronim disagree about the nature of the beit din's role in conversion. Some hold that the beit din is the one that accepts the convert in the name of all Israel, and so wrote Rav Shaul Yisraeli (Ḥavot Binyamin vol. 2, sha'ar 5, 67). With this he explained the law that conversions by "a beit din of laymen (hedyotot)" are valid (below 8), since the essence of conversion is the acceptance of the convert into the community of Israel. Several poskim likewise wrote that the will and consent of the beit din to accept the convert are required (Yeshu'ot Yisrael [Trunk] 3:2; Divrei Malkiel 2:77). Others say that it is the convert who converts, by accepting Jewish identity and the mitzvot, and the beit din only confirms this. So wrote Rav Rosenthal in Mishnat Ya'akov (Issurei Bi'ah 13:6). So too wrote Rav Feinstein (Dibrot Moshe, Yevamot 35:3), and on this basis he ruled that even public knowledge that the convert behaves as a Jew is effective to consider him a Jew. This also emerges from the words of Maharal Tzintz in Responsa Meshivat Nefesh (2:50), who wrote that even a presentation of one's intention to convert before three can be considered acceptance of the mitzvot. See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:8.

Regarding the fact that one cannot convert without a beit din, the Sages said in Kiddushin 62b: "A convert requires three; 'judgment' (mishpat) is written regarding him." And so too they said regarding the immersion, that it must be in the presence of a beit din (Yevamot 46b; 47b). On the other hand, we learned (Yevamot 45b) that Rav Assi validated a female convert on the basis of the argument: "Did she not immerse for her nidda?" That is, since it is known that she immersed for her nidda, she has thereby converted. The Rishonim asked: How does immersion for her nidda serve for her conversion, when it was not before three?
Some explained that immersion without the presence of a beit din is not effective for conversion, and the halakha does not follow Rav Assi (Behag); or that Rav Assi was referring to a special case in which she immersed for her nidda before three (Ritva and Nimukei Yosef).
In contrast, Tosafot (Yevamot 45b, s.v. "mi") answered that the presence of the beit din is indispensable only for the acceptance of the mitzvot, but the immersion is valid as long as it is known to have taken place, even if it was without the presence of a beit din, and this is what happened in the case of Rav Assi. So wrote the Mordekhai, Rosh, Agudah (Yevamot ibid.), Maharam of Rothenburg (ibid. 46b) and Ran (Kiddushin 26a in the Rif's pages). Tosafot there wrote an additional explanation: since it is known to all that she immersed for her nidda, her immersion is considered as if performed before a beit din.
Some say, according to the Rif and Rambam, that the immersion was not before a beit din and was for the sake of nidda, without explicit intention for conversion; and indeed, after the fact, immersion for nidda is effective for conversion, and the children of the female convert will be considered Jewish on the basis of this immersion. But one should not, ab initio, marry her without her immersing before a beit din for the sake of conversion. The case is one in which it is known in the community that she is accustomed to immerse for her nidda like a Jewish woman, or it is known that she conducts herself like a Jewish woman and consequently it is reasonable that she also immerses for her nidda, and therefore, in their view, this immersion of hers is considered conversion for her (so wrote, according to the Rif: Maharal Tzintz in Meshivat Nefesh 2:50. And so it appears to be the view of the Ramakh, Responsa Radbaz 4:86; Peraḥ Mateh Aharon 2:51, according to the Rif. And so is the view of the Tashbetz 3:227. And according to Tzafnat Pa'ane'aḥ, Issurei Bi'ah 13:9, and Dibrot Moshe, Yevamot 35:3, this is the view of the Rambam. See chapter 16 in Masoret Ha-giyur, that some say Jewish conduct can serve as a substitute for acceptance by the beit din). Others explain that her immersion for nidda cannot be effective for conversion, but in a case where it is not known whether the female convert underwent conversion properly, her immersion for nidda creates a ḥazaka (presumption) that she apparently converted according to halakha and immersed before three, and therefore her children are presumed to be Jewish. But since there are no witnesses to her conversion before a beit din, she may not be married without bringing witnesses that she converted according to halakha, or immersing before a beit din (so they explained according to the Rif and Rambam: Meiri, Maggid Mishneh in his main explanation, Mahari Ben Lev, Ranaḥ, Responsa Torat Emet 20, and Baḥ. And the Ramban and Ramakh explained the Rambam this way). The Ramban and Rashba (Yevamot 45b) explained the Rif along the lines of Tosafot, that there was acceptance of the mitzvot in a beit din before three, but since the immersion was not before three, one should not, ab initio, marry him.
The Shulḥan Arukh, 268:3, ruled without attribution like the view of Tosafot and Rosh, that even after the fact the acceptance of the mitzvot must be before three, but if he was circumcised or immersed not before three, or at night, the conversion is valid after the fact. And he mentioned the view of the Rif and Rambam by name, that without immersion before three, it is forbidden to marry into Israel.
Circumcision: According to many, the law of circumcision is like the law of immersion, and just as immersion must ab initio be before three, so must circumcision. And likewise regarding after the fact: just as the Rishonim disagree regarding immersion whether the conversion is valid when it was done not before three, so too regarding circumcision (Ramban, Tur, SA 268:3, and so it is implied by the Ritva). Some say that circumcision does not require three even ab initio (Baḥ in explaining the Rambam and Semag), just as for the circumcision of a Jew there is no requirement that three be present (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 267:4; 268:3). In practice, the Baḥ wrote that one should be concerned for the view of the Ramban, and he was cited by Maharam Schick YD 248 and many Aḥaronim.

sections.title_en: Who Is Fit to Serve as Judges
sections.body_en:
Ab initio, the judges of the conversion should be Torah scholars, so that they carry out the conversion according to halakha and properly weigh whether to accept the convert. After the fact, even if the judges of the conversion were not Torah scholars, as long as they were fit to testify, the conversion is valid. Those fit to testify are Torah-observant Jews who are not known to transgress deliberately any of the mitzvot of the Torah (below, halakha 9). Some say that even ab initio, Torah-observant Jews who are not Torah scholars may serve as the beit din for the entire conversion process, provided that one of them knows how to carry out the act of conversion according to halakha.

In practice, after the fact, if the judges were Torah-observant but not Torah scholars, the conversion has full validity. But ab initio, one should take care that the judges of the conversion be Torah scholars. And the custom of Israel is that the local rabbis are responsible for conversion, so that the acceptance of converts has the broad consent of the entire community. However, at the ceremony of the brit mila and the immersion, one may, even ab initio, make do with three fit Jews who serve as a beit din and supervise that the mitzva is performed according to halakha. This is because at the stage of circumcision and immersion the judges do not need to exercise discretion; rather, they continue the conversion process on the basis of the decision of the beit din that accepted the convert3

notes_en.en:
In Yevamot 46b it is explained that the judges of conversion do not need to be "mumḥim" (experts). According to most Rishonim, "mumḥim" are judges who received semikha (ordination) in an unbroken chain back to Moshe Rabbenu (Ramban, Rashba, Ritva, Tosafot Ha-Rosh ibid., and others). According to Rashi, mumḥim are "great Rabbis," that is, great Sages. The Gemara further explains later on (47b) that three Torah scholars inform the convert of some of the mitzvot at the time of the immersion. Thus the judges of the conversion must be Torah scholars, but they need not be ordained or great Sages. So too wrote the Meiri, Yevamot 46b, that the judges must be Torah scholars. And so it is implied by the words of many Rishonim, who wrote without qualification that conversion is carried out in the presence of Torah scholars, among them: Behag, Rif, Ra'avan, Ri (Tosafot Ri Ha-zaken, Kiddushin 62b), Riaz, Roke'aḥ, Rosh, Rabbenu Yeruḥam, Agudah. So too wrote the Tur (268:2): "And Torah scholars stand over his immersion and inform him." So too wrote the Rema 268:2, and many Aḥaronim cited his words, among them: Levush 2 and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 8. So too wrote Rav Ḥayim Palagi (Lev Ḥayim 3:28). And so wrote Rav Goren (Teḥumin 23, p. 171; Terumat Ha-goren 2:47), that one must take care that the judges of conversion be Torah scholars "holding ordination for halakhic instruction," for otherwise it is "a great stumbling block for the Torah and for Israel."
On the other hand, some hold that the judges of conversion need not be Torah scholars; rather, it suffices that they be fit Jews. So wrote the Rambam (Issurei Bi'ah 14:6) without qualification: "And three stand over him," which indicates that Torah scholars are not required. So too wrote the Semag, Orḥot Ḥayim, Yam Shel Shlomo (Yevamot 4:46), and Binyamin Ze'ev (1:72). So too wrote the SA 268:3: "All matters of the convert, whether informing him of the mitzvot to accept them, or the circumcision or the immersion, must be done by three who are fit to judge." And even laymen are fit to judge, as cited in SA ḤM 3:1: "And any three are called a beit din, even laymen." The Rema added there: "For it is impossible that there not be among them one who knows the reasoning of the laws. But if there is not among them one who knows, they are unfit to judge." Maharam Schick (YD 248) wrote that the intent is that one of them be "learned," that is, "knows the reasoning in that matter which we are judging." So too wrote Rav Ya'akov Sapir to Rav Natan Adler (Even Sapir vol. 2, p. 167), and he added that even according to the Rema (YD 268:2), who wrote that the judges should be Torah scholars, this is only "ab initio and as a mitzva, and even this only for the acceptance of the mitzvot … and not for the immersion." So too wrote the Rebbe Rayatz (Igrot vol. 9, letter 3268): "And he should choose two Jews who are Shabbat-observant and observant of mitzvot, from whom to make the members of the beit din." And so too wrote Igrot Moshe (YD 1:159), that even ab initio one may convert with three who are not Torah scholars, when one of them knows how to guide his colleagues in carrying out the conversion procedure.
To summarize, all agree that the judges of conversion need not be "mumḥim" (ordained or among the greatest Sages), and Rishonim and Aḥaronim disagree whether the judges must be Torah scholars. After the fact, it is agreed that as long as the people are fit to testify, that is, Torah-observant Jews who are not known to transgress deliberately any of the mitzvot of the Torah, the conversion is valid (below, halakha 9). And although, according to the basic law, any three Torah scholars can establish a beit din and convert, the custom of Israel is that the local rabbis are responsible for conversion, so that the acceptance of converts has the broad consent of the entire community, similar to what R. Gershom the Circumciser wrote in the Rules of Circumcision (Zikhron Brit La-rishonim, p. 133): "And three Torah scholars or three of the dignitaries of the city are required, who stand over the convert."

sections.title_en: It Is a Mitzva to Accept Righteous Converts
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to draw near and convert righteous converts (gerei tzedek), and therefore the Sages said that once it is known that the convert's desire to convert is a genuine desire, the conversion should not be delayed, for one should not tarry in fulfilling the mitzva (Yevamot 47b). Included in this mitzva is accompanying and teaching the righteous convert in preparation for his acceptance by the beit din. This mitzva is included in the mitzva of loving God and in the mitzva of loving one's fellow creatures.

Loving God, as it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might." The Sages said (ibid. in the Sifrei): "'And you shall love the Lord' – make Him beloved to His creatures," in the way that Avraham our father and Sarah our mother would draw converts near, as it is stated (Bereishit 12:5): "And the souls that they had made in Ḥaran." And what is meant by "made"? "Surely if all the inhabitants of the world gathered together to create a single gnat and put a soul into it, they could not!" So how could Avraham and Sarah make souls? "Rather, it teaches you that whoever draws a convert near, it is as if he created him … Avraham would convert the men and Sarah would convert the women" (Bereishit Rabba 39:14; 84:4).

Loving one's fellow creatures, because conversion involves an act of kindness toward the convert, who through conversion will merit to enter under the wings of the Shekhina and be elevated to the stature of Israel. Therefore, all those who help converts to convert fulfill thereby the mitzva of "And you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Vayikra 19:18), on top of which a special mitzva was added to love the convert, as it is stated (Devarim 10:19): "And you shall love the convert, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (above 1:1).4

notes_en.en: In the Azharot of R. Yitzḥak Albargeloni it is written that accepting converts is included in the mitzva of loving the convert, and Rav Perla wrote that it is included in the mitzva of loving God. Admittedly, those who enumerated the mitzvot did not count this mitzva, apparently because it is a general mitzva that includes all the mitzvot. In any case, it is agreed that it is a mitzva to accept converts, as the Ra'avad wrote (Ba'alei Ha-nefesh, end of Sha'ar Ha-tevila), that therefore, when a minor convert is immersed, one recites before his immersion: "and commanded us concerning immersion." Similarly, Tosafot Ha-Rosh (Yevamot 109b) wrote that when a convert makes an effort to convert, the beit din must accept him, and refusing to accept him is a sin for which one may be punished, just as Israel was punished because the Patriarchs did not accept Timna, from whom came Amalek, who caused Israel suffering (Sanhedrin 99b).

sections.title_en: Conversion for the Sake of Benefits
sections.body_en:
Conversion must be for the sake of Heaven, that is, out of identification with Judaism; but if the gentile seeks to convert not for the sake of Heaven, he should not be accepted. Therefore, the beit din must clarify for what purpose the gentile has come to convert. If it becomes clear that he wishes to convert for the sake of marriage, that is, in order to marry a Jewish woman, or to improve his economic situation, he should not be accepted, since his conversion is not for the sake of Heaven. Therefore the Sages said (Yevamot 24b): "Converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah," for then there is concern that the conversion is for the sake of honor and money. "Similarly, converts were not accepted either in the days of David or in the days of Shlomo." In the days of David, because they sought to convert out of fear of his armies, and in the days of Shlomo, because they sought to convert in order to share in the wealth of Israel. The Sages likewise said that "lion converts and dream converts" are not accepted, that is, people who do not identify with Judaism but come to convert out of fear – so that lions not kill them, or because an angel warned them in a dream to convert in order to be saved from calamity.

However, even in times when Israel merits wealth and honor, if the beit din has the impression that the convert's intention is for the sake of Heaven, he is accepted. Thus in the days of David they accepted Ittai the Gittite, for since he was wealthy and distinguished, it was clear that he came to convert for the sake of Heaven. It is likewise related (Menaḥot 44a) that they converted a woman who came to convert for the sake of marriage, because it became clear from her story that her main intention was for the sake of Heaven (Tosafot Yevamot 24b, s.v. "lo").5

If the beit din, deliberately or inadvertently, transgressed and accepted converts who did not come for the sake of Heaven, according to Rabbi Neḥemya their conversion has no validity. However, according to halakha, although ab initio one should not accept a convert who converts for the sake of marriage, if they accepted him, his conversion is a valid conversion, as explained in the Mishna (Yevamot 24b; SA YD 268:12. See above 3:9, note 8, regarding the conversion of the Kutim – the Samaritans).

notes_en.en: In Menaḥot 44a it is related that there was a wealthy harlot in one of the cities overseas who would charge four hundred gold coins as her fee. Once a Jew sought to sin with her; he paid her fee, but in the end, by the merit of the mitzva of tzitzit, he refrained from sinning with her. This aroused her admiration, and she asked that he write down for her his name, his place of residence and the name of his teacher. "She arose and divided all her property: a third to the government (so that they would allow her to convert), a third to the poor (to atone for her sins), and a third she took in her hand, apart from those bedspreads, and she came to the study hall of R. Ḥiya. She said to him: Rabbi, instruct them concerning me and let them make me a convert. He said to her: My daughter, perhaps you have set your eyes on one of the students?" – for he was concerned that perhaps she had not found a groom among her own people and had come to convert in order to marry one of the students, and not for the sake of Heaven. "She took out the note from her hand and gave it to him," and in the letter the incident was recorded, and from it one could understand that she was wealthy and could easily have chosen a gentile groom, but she chose the student because of his greatness of spirit. Since this was so, he agreed to convert her. "He said to her: Go, take possession of your acquisition! Those very bedspreads that she had spread for him in prohibition, she spread for him in permission." From here Tosafot (Yevamot 24b, s.v. "lo") learned that if the main intention of the conversion is for the sake of Heaven, one converts even when the conversion is for the sake of marriage. See further in Masoret Ha-giyur 2:2-6.

sections.title_en: The Dilemma of the Beit Din
sections.body_en:
In order to understand the great dilemma that faces the beit din when it comes to decide on accepting a convert, let us return to the fundamentals. The purpose of conversion is to join the people of Israel, the people of God, whose destiny is to walk in the ways of God and to bring blessing to all the families of the earth. For this purpose God gave His people Israel His Torah and His mitzvot, through whose fulfillment it will merit His light and His blessing and will be able to repair the world.

The problem is that the beit din has no ability to know with certainty whether the convert wishes to convert out of faith in God and a desire to fulfill mitzvot, or whether he wishes to convert for the sake of benefits or in order to regularize his marriage. And although the convert declares his faith in God and his desire to fulfill mitzvot, the judges are unable to search the heart and mind and know whether he is speaking truth or falsehood, or whether his words are divided – partly true and partly false. And even in a case where the judges are inclined to think that the convert is speaking the truth, they are unable to know whether in practice the convert will withstand the difficulties involved in integrating into the people of Israel and in fulfilling the mitzvot, or whether, because of weakness of character or the difficulties he will encounter, he will weaken in his faith and stop fulfilling mitzvot, and perhaps even return to his previous identity. And conversely, even when the judges are inclined to suspect that the convert is lying, and he does not truly identify with Judaism and does not intend to fulfill mitzvot, and his request to convert is in order to regularize his marriage or his status in Israel, it is possible that over time, living among Israel, he will progress gradually to the level of a righteous convert. Experience, too, teaches that it is hard to predict the future, for there were converts who at first were very enthusiastic about Judaism, and after their conversion reverted to their old ways. And there were converts who appeared indifferent to Judaism, and were accepted with difficulty only because they were already living with a Jewish spouse, and after the conversion, in a gradual process, they grew greatly stronger until they became great tzaddikim.

If, in order to avoid accepting converts who will not be righteous converts, the beit din agrees to convert only converts who are almost certain to be righteous converts, it will sin by rejecting many converts who could have been righteous converts, and will cause great harm to the people of Israel. For the Sages said (Pesaḥim 87b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them"; thus rejecting a convert prolongs the exile and delays the redemption. Moreover, refusing to accept a convert whose soul is rooted in Israel may cause great danger to Israel, for this is a great soul that has not found its rectification, and it may turn to evil. As the Sages said about Timna, who was a princess and wished to cleave to the seed of Avraham our father and to convert. However, the Patriarchs rejected her, apparently because they sensed that her character traits were not good. She went and became a concubine to Elifaz the son of Esav, and from her was born Amalek, who caused Israel suffering. From here the Sages learned that after Timna came back and asked again and again to convert, the Patriarchs should have converted her and not pushed her away (Sanhedrin 99b; Bereishit Rabba 82:14). We have likewise learned that as a result of Avraham our father's negligence in converting the people of Sedom, it was decreed upon his descendants that they be enslaved in Egypt (Nedarim 32a; above 1:9, note 5).

On the other hand, if the beit din persuades gentiles to convert, or is lenient in converting anyone who asks, it will cause great harm to Israel by accepting converts who will continue to identify as gentiles and to behave according to their customs, and will influence for the worse their friends and neighbors, who will learn from their ways. Regarding such converts the Sages said (Yevamot 47b): "Converts are as difficult for Israel as a sapaḥat (a skin affliction)" (above 1:11, note 7), and regarding those who accept such converts they said (Yevamot 109b): "Evil after evil will come upon those who accept converts."

Many times the reality is complex: the convert's intention is not sufficiently for the sake of Heaven, and there is indeed concern that his conversion will cause troubles and complications, and perhaps he and his family members will influence their Jewish friends for the worse. However, there is also a chance that after a long and painful process, he and his descendants will become integrated into Israel and absorb the faith of Israel, and great and righteous people will come forth from them.

sections.title_en: The Approaches of Shammai and Hillel
sections.body_en:
The decision of the beit din also depends on the character and life experience of the judges. If they are inclined toward kindness and their approach is optimistic, or if they have encountered righteous converts in the past, they will tend to look upon the convert favorably and to believe that his intention is good, and they will accept him. And if they are inclined toward the attribute of strict judgment and their stance is sober and pessimistic, or if they have encountered in the past converts who turned out to be alienated from Israel and from the mitzvot, they will tend to doubt the convert's intention and will not agree to accept him.

Similarly, it is related in the Talmud (Shabbat 31a) about a certain gentile who came before Shammai and asked him: How many Torahs do you have? Shammai answered him: Two – the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. He said to him: The Written one – I believe you; but the Oral one – I do not believe you. Convert me on condition that you teach me the Written Torah. Shammai rebuked him and sent him away in reproach. He came before Hillel – he converted him and began to teach him, until he accepted upon himself the Oral Torah as well.

Another incident: a gentile came before Shammai the Elder and asked to convert on condition that he teach him the entire Torah while standing on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit (measuring rod) that was in his hand, for how is it possible to teach the entire Torah on one foot?! As for his pushing him away with a builder's cubit – this is because such was the way of the greatest Sages: as long as they did not serve in public positions, they made their living from their own work. Hillel was a woodcutter and Shammai was a builder. By pushing the gentile away with the builder's cubit, with which he would straighten his building, Shammai hinted to him that his request was improper and deviated from the straight path. That gentile came before Hillel; he agreed to convert him, and said to him: What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow – this is the entire Torah on one foot, and all the rest of the words of the Torah are explanations and ramifications of this great foundation, and you must go on to study them in order to fulfill the Torah.

Another incident: a certain gentile heard about the garments of the High Priest and was impressed by his honor and by the splendid beauty of his garments. He came before Shammai and asked to convert on condition that he be appointed High Priest. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's cubit that was in his hand, for one who was not born a kohen cannot be a High Priest. When he came before Hillel with the same request, Hillel accepted him and converted him, and told him that since he wishes to be a great man in Israel, he must study "the protocols of royalty," that is, the Torah. When the convert reached the verse in which it is explained that even Israelites cannot serve in the priesthood, he reasoned a kal va-ḥomer (a fortiori) regarding himself and understood that a convert cannot be High Priest, and he agreed to be an ordinary Jew.

The Sages concluded their story by relating that some time later these three converts happened to come together in one place, and they said: "Shammai's impatience sought to drive us from the world; Hillel's humility brought us near, under the wings of the Shekhina." Seemingly, according to the letter of the law, Shammai was right in not accepting these three converts, for according to their own words they did not accept the Torah and the mitzvot. In addition, it is reasonable that in contrast to those three converts whom Shammai rejected and Hillel accepted and who turned out to be righteous converts, there were cases in which Hillel accepted converts who afterward reverted to their old ways, and it turned out that Shammai had been right. However, from the fact that the Gemara chose to bring the story of the converts whom Hillel accepted and who turned out to be righteous converts, it is implied that it is preferable to follow the approach of Hillel. That is, although it is clear that there is room for the approach of Shammai, and every rabbi who resembles Shammai in his character and worldview should be faithful to his own way, the Gemara wished to teach us that the way of Hillel is preferable.

In the course of this we have learned that a convert, too, is permitted to choose to convert with rabbis who follow the way of Hillel, and even if he sought to convert with one rabbi who did not accept him, he may go to convert with another rabbi. And likewise a rabbi is permitted to accept a convert who was rejected by another rabbi.

sections.title_en: Everything According to the Judgment of the Beit Din
sections.body_en:
Since the beit din cannot know with certainty what is in the heart of the one converting, and cannot predict how the convert and his descendants will behave in the future, the beit din must weigh all the considerations and decide according to its discretion. That is, there is almost always some doubt whether it is right to accept the convert or to reject him, and the responsibility and the authority to decide according to what seems right in its eyes rests with the beit din, in accordance with the famous rule: "Everything is according to the judgment of the beit din" (Beit Yosef 268:12; Shakh 23).

There are situations in which the poskim disagree as to how far the beit din may use its authority and convert a convert regarding whom there is serious concern that his conversion is not for the sake of Heaven. Some are stringent and hold that when there is a well-founded doubt whether the one seeking to convert does not intend it for the sake of Heaven, it is obligatory to reject him, and the matter is not left to the discretion of the beit din. This, they say, is what the Sages (Yevamot 24b) meant in their instruction not to accept a convert who wishes to marry a Jewish woman, and not to accept converts at a time when Israel lives in wealth, for in these cases there is serious concern that the conversion is for the sake of marriage or money, and not for the sake of Heaven. Only when it seems very likely to the beit din that the convert's main intention is for the sake of Heaven and he intends to fulfill mitzvot with devotion, even though there is also a motive of marriage or money, may it exercise discretion and accept him.

On the other hand, some are lenient and hold that even where there is a well-founded concern that the convert's intention is not for the sake of Heaven, for instance he wishes to marry a Jewish woman or to improve his economic situation, if the beit din assesses that there is a chance that the convert will progress and become a righteous convert, it may convert him. Likewise, if through the conversion his partner will preserve her Jewish identity and be saved from assimilation, the beit din may decide to convert him, even though his main intention is to convert for the sake of marriage or money. For what the Sages said – not to convert for the sake of marriage or money – applies specifically when the convert's entire intention is for the sake of marriage or money; but if he also has an intention for the sake of Heaven, it is permitted to convert him. They further explained that not accepting converts for the sake of marriage is good guidance but not binding law, and when there is a special need for it in order to save from assimilation, or when the judges also see a good intention in the one converting, it is within their authority to decide to convert him even though the main motive for the conversion is not for the sake of Heaven.6

notes_en.en:
As we learned in the previous halakha, Shammai rejected converts who, according to their own declaration, did not intend to convert for the sake of Heaven but rather in order to wear the garments of the High Priest, or did not intend to observe the mitzvot properly but only the Written Torah or what can be learned on one foot. Hillel, however, accepted them, because he assessed that they would be righteous converts. So too wrote Tosafot (Yevamot 24b, s.v. "lo"), that Hillel converted them because "Hillel was confident that in the end he would act for the sake of Heaven." Admittedly, Teshurat Shai 1:526 wrote that Hillel relied on divine inspiration (ru'aḥ ha-kodesh), but the view of the vast majority of the poskim is that Hillel relied on his own assessment that they would be righteous converts, and not on divine inspiration, for it is known that one does not decide halakha according to divine inspiration (Bava Metzia 59b), and consequently he knew that it was possible that perhaps they would not be righteous converts. So wrote Rav Tzirelson (Atzei Ha-levanon YD 63); Pri Ha-sadeh 2:3; Rav Mordekhai Eidelberg (Ḥazon La-mo'ed 6); Yabi'a Omer vol. 11, YD 28. See Masoret Ha-giyur 2:3-4. And there, 2:6, it is explained that when there is doubt whether the convert intends it for the sake of Heaven, some hold that the beit din is forbidden to accept him (Yad Ha-levi 1, YD 145; Beit She'arim YD 361). And some say that it is within their authority to convert him (Rav Eliyahu Guttmacher in Aderet Eliyahu YD 87; Pri Ha-sadeh 2:3; 71; Mishpetei Uziel vol. 2, YD 53). Rav Bleich explained (see Masoret Ha-giyur 25:3) that the words of the Sages (Yevamot 24b) not to convert for the sake of marriage and money are good advice and not binding halakha.
See further in Masoret Ha-giyur 2:5; 7-8, that the poskim disagree whether the rule "Everything is according to the judgment of the beit din" is a broad rule, which grants the judges extensive authority to accept converts whenever they believe that this is beneficial for the community of Israel or for saving the Jewish partner from assimilation; or whether the rule is limited to a case where there is doubt regarding the intentions of the convert himself, but when it is clear that he comes for the sake of marriage and the like, he is not to be accepted, except in special cases in which it is clear that his intention is for the sake of Heaven (see Aseh Lekha Rav 3:29). This dispute is part of the great dispute whether, in order to prevent assimilation, one may convert non-Jewish partners who are not expected to keep a religious way of life but rather to live with a "Jewish identity" alone (below 6:4-6).

sections.body_en:
As we learned (in halakha 4), the Sages said (Yevamot 24b): "Converts were not accepted either in the days of David or in the days of Shlomo." In the days of David because of the concern that they sought to convert out of fear of his armies, and in the days of Shlomo because of the concern that they sought to convert in order to share in the wealth of Israel. But this is difficult, for the Sages said (Yevamot 79a) that in the days of David and Shlomo one hundred and fifty thousand converts were converted, who saw how Israel treated the Givonite converts with honor and asked to convert, and they were the ones who helped Shlomo prepare the materials for building the Temple (above 3:7).

The Rambam explained (Issurei Bi'ah 13:15) that indeed the official batei din did not accept converts in the days of David and Shlomo; however, many converts would convert "before laymen, and the Great Beit Din was wary of them: they did not reject them, since they had immersed in any case, nor did they draw them near until their end would be seen" (and so wrote the Ramban and Rashba). According to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, there was no doubt about the validity of the conversion, for after the fact laymen are fit to convert; and what is meant by the Great Beit Din not drawing them near until it would see how they behaved is that they did not rely on their trustworthiness regarding kashrut, or that they recommended not marrying them, until they would see that they conducted themselves according to halakha.7

The poskim disagree as to what the attitude of the Great Beit Din was toward those batei din of laymen that converted the one hundred and fifty thousand converts. Some say that the Great Beit Din opposed their converting improperly, but since, after the fact, any Jew who is fit to testify is fit to serve as a judge for conversion, the conversion performed by the laymen was valid (Kesef Mishneh, Issurei Bi'ah 13:15; Ezrat Kohen 14).

And some say that the beit din did not oppose the conversions of the batei din of laymen, but rather preferred to turn a blind eye to their conversions, and perhaps even supported them silently. For it is impossible that it opposed and protested against them and nevertheless they converted one hundred and fifty thousand contrary to its position. Rather, its position was that it is not fitting for the Sages to convert converts who come to convert for the sake of security and wealth, but on the other hand, it is also not fitting to reject them. Therefore it preferred that laymen convert them, for they are permitted to respond to such converts and convert them (Maggid Mishneh, Issurei Bi'ah 13:14; Aderet Eliyahu YD 87).8

notes_en.en: Admittedly, some hold that according to the Rambam, if they did not fulfill mitzvot after their conversion, the Great Beit Din would annul their conversion or would cast doubt on it (Ḥazon Naḥum vol. 1, 90:5; Or Le-Tzion vol. 1, YD 12). And some say that if they continued to engage in idolatry, it would annul their conversion (Avnei Tzedek EH 27; 80, as cited in Masoret Ha-giyur 7:19-20). However, according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, the Rambam did not cast doubt on the conversion of the laymen, as emerges from his words regarding the wives of Shlomo and Shimshon (Issurei Bi'ah 13:17). And what is meant by "they were wary of them" is that they did not rely on their trustworthiness regarding kashrut; so wrote Rav Eliyahu Guttmacher, Rav Yeḥezkel Banet, Rav Mas'ud Ha-kohen (Pirḥei Kehuna EH 10), and many others. Or that they were wary of marrying them until their end would be seen; so wrote Rav Glasner (Ḥakor Davar p. 13); Nehar Mitzrayim (Hilkhot Gerim 4); Rav Herzog (Heikhal Yitzḥak EH 1, 20:7), and others, as cited in Masoret Ha-giyur 7:21.

The Maggid Mishneh wrote (Issurei Bi'ah 13:14): "Our Master [the Rambam] explained that a beit din of laymen would convert them, and after the fact they are all converts." The Kesef Mishneh (ibid., halakha 15) understood from his words that in his view a beit din of laymen may convert even converts who come for the sake of something else, and only regular batei din are forbidden to accept such converts. However, the Kesef Mishneh himself disagreed with him and explained that laymen, too, are forbidden to convert for the sake of something else, and the laymen who converted in the days of David and Shlomo acted not in accordance with halakha, but after the fact their conversions are conversions. So too wrote Rav Kook (Ezrat Kohen 14); Rav Tzvi Hirsch Grodzensky (Ha-me'asef 16, 2, 20); and Rav Dov Abramovitz (Dat Yisrael vol. 2, p. 153).
On the other hand, some hold that laymen are permitted to convert for the sake of marriage, in accordance with the view of the Maggid Mishneh as understood by the Kesef Mishneh, and therefore the Great Beit Din did not protest against the laymen who converted one hundred and fifty thousand converts in the days of David and Shlomo. So wrote Rav Ḥayim Bleich (cited in Masoret Ha-giyur 25:3). Similarly wrote Rav Eliyahu Guttmacher (Aderet Eliyahu YD 87) and Rav Uziel (Mishpetei Uziel 7:18). And Rav Yissakhar Tamar (Alei Tamar, Kiddushin 4:1, s.v. "ha-mitgayrim") explained that the Great Beit Din saw that the public was accepting those who sought to convert, and understood that if it did not allow their conversion, "there exists a serious concern of division of the nation and a rift in the unity of the people," and therefore it preferred to turn a blind eye to their conversions. Similarly, Rav Feinstein explained that since these seekers of conversion had in any case begun to intermingle with Israel, the Great Beit Din preferred that laymen convert them (Dibrot Moshe, Yevamot, end of 35). And Rav Yisrael Porat wrote that the laymen represent the masses of the people, who seek out converts, whereas the Sages do not seek out converts but also do not prevent the laymen from accepting them (Mizraḥ U-ma'arav 1, 5-6, pp. 378-380).
Following from this, some hold that when the conversion is for the sake of marriage, and there is a need to convert in order to prevent assimilation, it is preferable that the conversion be carried out by a beit din of laymen. So wrote Rav Yosef Mashash (Otzar Ha-mikhtavim 2, 1830); Menaḥem Meshiv 1:42; Ḥedvat Ya'akov YD 13; Rav David Tzvi Katzburg (Tel Talpiyot vol. 9, p. 231); Rav Yosef Lipland (Gerim Ve-geirut, siman 1); Me'orot Natan 108; Be'er Ḥayim Mordekhai vol. 1, YD 40. See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:13. On the other hand, according to Rav Ḥayim David Halevi (Aseh Lekha Rav 3:29), it is preferable that regular batei din convert them "with great caution," and not "abandon" the matter to the hands of laymen.
It should further be noted that although the baraita in Yevamot 24b states that "converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah," it is explained in the Prophets that converts will convert in the days of the Messiah, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 14:1): "For the Lord will have mercy on Ya'akov, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land; and the stranger shall join himself with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Ya'akov." And the Radak explained: "'And will yet choose Israel' – in the days of the Messiah, and then 'the stranger shall join himself' with them, as it is written (Zekharya 2:15): 'And many nations shall join themselves to the Lord on that day, and they shall be My people.'" And several of the great Aḥaronim wrote that in the future, batei din of laymen will convert gentiles who wish to join Israel. So wrote the Ḥida (Tzavarei Shalal, haftarat Beha'alotekha, letter 2), and Rav Ḥayim Katzavi in his book Tzror Ha-ḥayim (Berakhot 57b). See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:10.

sections.title_en: A Valid and an Invalid Beit Din
sections.body_en:
As we learned (in halakha 2), ab initio the judges of conversion should be Torah scholars; however, after the fact, even Jews who are not Torah scholars are fit to be judges for conversion. This is the rule: anyone who is disqualified from being a witness in one of the official testimonies of the Torah, such as testimony for marriage or divorce, is disqualified from being a judge for conversion. And who is disqualified from testimony? One who is considered "wicked" with regard to one of the mitzvot, as it is stated (Shemot 23:1): "Do not put your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness" (Sanhedrin 27a). That is, one who is known to transgress deliberately one of the mitzvot of the Torah. For example, a thief is disqualified from testimony, and if he returned the stolen item and repented fully of it, he becomes fit for testimony again. Similarly, if one of the judges of the conversion is known to take bribes, his conversions are invalid (see Baḥ ḤM 9:9). Likewise one who desecrates Shabbat or eats non-kosher food is disqualified from testimony, and if he repented, he becomes fit for testimony again (SA ḤM 34).

Therefore the poskim ruled that Reform, and even Conservative, conversion is invalid, since the converting judges do not observe all the mitzvot.9

When the Sages of a certain place enacted an ordinance that one may not convert there without certain conditions, as was done in the community of Sephardic Jews from Aleppo in Argentina, if Sages or laymen arose and converted contrary to the conditions they set, according to most poskim their conversions are valid. Admittedly, under certain conditions the representatives of the public may impose fines on those who convert contrary to the ordinances of the community, but they cannot invalidate the conversion, since it was carried out by Torah-observant Jews, whose status is at the very least that of laymen.10

notes_en.en:
The poskim ruled that Reform or Conservative conversion is invalid. And even if the judges are learned, lovers of Israel and pious in many mitzvot, since there are mitzvot that, by force of their principled position, they do not observe, they are considered transgressors who are disqualified, like the law of witnesses who are known to transgress one of the mitzvot of the Torah, who are disqualified from official testimony of the Torah. This is the view of Aḥi'ezer vol. 3, 26:6; Rav Goren in Terumat Ha-goren 2:49; Rav Yitzḥak Ḥazan in Yeḥaveh Da'at vol. 3, EH 18; Igrot Moshe EH 3:3; Rav Menaḥem Mendel Schneerson in Torat Menaḥem 5730, 60. In addition, Igrot Moshe (YD 1:160; EH 3:3) wrote that the judges must believe in the foundations of the Jewish faith, and one who does not believe in them is disqualified for conversion. And some invalidated their conversions also because they assessed that the act of conversion itself was carried out not in accordance with halakha. See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:14. And there were rabbis who regarded Conservative or Reform conversion as a doubtful conversion, as Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu responded (Responsa of the Chief Rabbi 5748-5749, 231) regarding a couple who converted in a Reform conversion and married in a Reform marriage and are asking to be accepted into an Orthodox community: they should be converted together with their children as a stringency, without blessings, and likewise married as a stringency, without blessings. Likewise, in Responsa Pri Ha-sadeh vol. 2, 71, he was in doubt regarding the validity of the conversion of a convert who converted with Neologs, and in Responsa She'ilat Moshe 95 he was in doubt regarding the validity of a Reform conversion because perhaps the immersion was not before three. See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:15.
Several poskim further wrote that when a gentile has undergone a Reform conversion, it is fitting to be lenient in converting him and even to do so promptly, both because he has already begun to identify with the Jewish people, and in order to prevent the error of Jews who will think that he is Jewish when in truth his conversion did not take effect. So wrote Responsa She'ilat Moshe 95; Responsa Maharam Brisk 1:1; Rav Kunstadt in Responsa Ya'aneh Barukh 54.

Above, in note 3, it was explained that the judges of conversion need not be mumḥim and ordained. The Ramban, Rashba and Ritva explained that the acceptance of converts is considered "judgment" (mishpat) with regard to the requirement of three judges, but not with regard to the requirement that the judges be mumḥim and ordained. The Ramban, Rashba and R. Netanel in Tosafot (Kiddushin 62b, s.v. "ger") further wrote that we learned (Keritot 9a) that conversion is "for your generations," that is, it applies always, in all generations, even after semikha ceased. On the other hand, some say that the judges of conversion must be ordained, like the judges who are fit for many laws of the Torah, such as laws of punishments, fines and sanctifying the month. And nowadays, when semikha has ceased, conversion takes place by virtue of acting as agents of the ordained judges of the past (Tosafot Yevamot 47a, s.v. "mishpat"). And they asked: But we learned that one judges as agents of the ordained judges only in laws that are commonly needed (Gittin 88b). Tosafot explained (ibid., s.v. "be-milta") that conversion is considered a common matter. And the Ran explained that although conversion is not common, because of the great necessity "to bring a person under the wings of the Shekhina," it is imperative to carry it out as agents of the early ordained judges (and so wrote the Sema, ḤM 1:3).
Some of the Aḥaronim were concerned for the reasoning that conversion is by virtue of "agency," and ruled that if the conversion was carried out contrary to the guidance of the Sages, for instance they accepted a convert who came for the sake of marriage, since the judges betrayed their agency, there is room to say that their conversion is void (Rav Shalom Kutna). However, many ruled that even if the judges converted contrary to the guidance of the Sages, their conversion is valid. Either because conversion is not based on agency, as the Or Same'aḥ (Issurei Bi'ah 14:13) learned from the fact that, after the fact, conversion for the sake of marriage is valid, even though the one who converted betrayed the agency of the Sages, who instructed not to convert for the sake of marriage. And so wrote Piskei Uziel Bi-she'elot Ha-zman 61, and others. Or because the agency is not annulled when the instructions of the Sages were transgressed, as long as the Sages did not establish that in such a manner the conversion is void. And they brought proof from the fact that although the Sages forbade the immersion of a convert on Shabbat, after the fact, if he transgressed and immersed, the conversion is valid (Beit Yitzḥak YD vol. 2, 100:5). See Masoret Ha-giyur 11:5-7.
When they transgressed and converted contrary to the ordinance of the community in a certain place, as in the community of Sephardic Jews from Aleppo in Argentina, according to Rav Ḥizkiya Shabtai their conversions are void, and Rav Frank did not agree to annul them, but held that one who converted there must convert again due to the doubt. However, according to Rav Uziel, Rav Herzog and Rav Ovadia Yosef, the conversions contrary to the ordinance are valid, and so is the view of most poskim, as explained in Masoret Ha-giyur 27:7.
